title: Gusuku, Paddy and Runway: Chatan and the Base That Split a Village
standfirst: On Okinawa's central-west coast, a coral-limestone castle, the island's finest rice paddies and a sixteenth-century sweet potato all mark ground that the US landing of 1 April 1945 remade overnight. An airfield cut the old village in two, bases still cover roughly half the town, and a returned airstrip became the shopping streets of American Village.

sections.heading: A castle, a monk and a sweet potato

paragraphs.text: Chatan occupies a stretch of low coral-limestone coast in central Okinawa, and its oldest visible monument sits on a low, tongue-shaped ridge above the shore: Chatan Gusuku, a fortified hilltop about 500 metres long whose five walled enclosures once housed a regional power of the Chuzan kingdom. Japan's Agency for Cultural Affairs, which designated the ruin a national Historic Site in March 2021, dates its main building phase from the late thirteenth to the early sixteenth century and records finds of imported trade ceramics among its cut and roughly coursed limestone walls; the town's own account of the site calls it a connected-compound gusuku of four aligned terraces, among the largest such castles on the island.

The old district's name is itself a small piece of history. A 1649 map submitted to the shogunate by the Satsuma domain labels the local magiri, or district, with the kana "kitatan", which the town's own history traces sliding over generations through "kichatan" and "chichatan" into today's "Chatan" — "tan", in the dialect of Kagoshima officials who compiled the map, simply meaning valley. A charter is said to mention the name as early as 1577. By the sixteenth century the magiri comprised twelve hamlets strung along the coast and inland, among them Chatan itself, Kuwae, Yara and Noguni, all of which would remain one administrative unit until the twentieth century.

One of those hamlets gave Okinawa a food staple. A history of Ryukyu's "five great men", printed in 1916, credits Noguni Sokan — a title meaning simply "the intendant from Noguni" — with carrying the sweet potato back from China in 1605, during the reign of King Sho Nei; the book itself notes that scholars already argued over whether someone else had beaten him to it, but records that in 1764 the kingdom formally commended his achievement. A generation or so later, Chatan's Tamayose hamlet produced a monk remembered as "the Elder of Chatan": ordained Nan'yo Shoko, he studied in mainland Japan around 1603 and returned, a 1937 guide to Okinawa records, as one of the channels through which mainland Japanese learning reached the Ryukyu court.

sections.heading: The finest rice paddies in the prefecture

paragraphs.text: For most of its history before 1945, Chatan was known not for castles or monks but for water. The magiri's twelve hamlets became twelve numbered "aza" in 1908, when Okinawa's old magiri were reorganized into villages on the Japanese pattern, and Chatan village prospered as a farming community built around a lowland that three of its hamlets — Chatan, Tamashiro and Dendo — shared: paddies the town's own history calls the "Chatan Tabukwa", ranked among the three finest rice-growing tracts in the whole prefecture. It is a landscape that has almost entirely vanished, and one reason this dossier's aerial photographs are worth studying closely for the traces reclamation and construction have left across the lowland.

Kadena, on the northern edge of the old magiri, grew into Nakagami district's own hub in these decades: Kadena's own history describes it hosting the terminus of the prefectural railway, a prefectural middle school, an agricultural school and a sugar mill, all serving a wide rural hinterland that still belonged, administratively, to Chatan village.

sections.heading: Invasion and a village cut in two

paragraphs.text: War reached Chatan before the main invasion did. Japan's national record of civilian war dead, compiled by the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, records 33 people killed in Chatan village in the air raid of 10 October 1944, the day US carrier aircraft struck targets across Okinawa; the same record dates the main invasion precisely, noting that American forces landed "around Chatan village" on 1 April 1945, part of a landing that ran along the coast from Yomitan through Kadena and into Chatan. Within days the old rice paddies and farmland were being cleared for what would become Kadena air base, and the prefectural archives' own account of the town's occupation describes its residential areas as comprehensively destroyed.

The airfield did something no natural disaster had: it cut the village bureaucratically in half. By 1948, expanding US management of the runway had closed off all passage across it, so that residents on the airfield's far side had to travel by way of Naha or central Okinawa simply to reach their own village office. On 4 December 1948, with a population of about 3,800, the northern hamlets separated to form Kadena village — an administrative divorce forced, in effect, by the base itself; Kadena would go on to become Nakagami district's seventh town, in January 1976.

Recovery in what remained of Chatan depended in part on connections built by decades of emigration. Okinawa's prefectural archives record a Hawaii-based relief and rehabilitation society helping the devastated community between 1947 and 1951, years in which contested land claims — farmland whose boundaries and ownership records had been destroyed along with the houses that stood on it — were the subject of public hearings in 1951; the same records note a further wave of emigration from Chatan to Brazil, Peru and Bolivia through the 1950s and 1960s, as base employment only slowly replaced the vanished rice economy.

sections.heading: Two-thirds of a town under fences

paragraphs.text: When Okinawa reverted to Japanese administration in 1972, US bases still covered about 65 percent of Chatan's land, according to a National Archives of Japan account of the town drawn from its own administrative records; only 11,496 residents were left to live on the remaining third. A similar figure — 68 percent of the town under military use, with base-related work accounting for the great majority of a local economy in which services alone made up 86 percent of output — appears in the town's own retrospective on the era of Mayor Higa, when Chatan drew up its first village promotion plan in 1974, a ten-year programme aimed at 1981. Chatan gained formal town status in 1980, still governing a community whose developable land was a minority of its own territory.

Return, when it came, came from the coast. In 1981 the US military gave up Hamby Airfield, a small strip on the western shore, together with the inland May-Moscarella firing range — the two returns the town's own planning report of 2004 calls the point at which "prospects for the town's development opened wide" after decades of being penned in. Even so, as of the town's own 2018 accounting, Kadena Air Base, Camp Kuwae, part of Camp Zukeran and an Army fuel depot together still occupied about 51.6 percent of Chatan's 13.91 square kilometres, leaving 7.2 square kilometres for everything else the town does.

sections.heading: From Hamby Airfield to American Village

paragraphs.text: The returned airstrip did not stay empty. A land readjustment project turned the old Hamby site into the Kitamae district, and from 1988 new landfill was raised along the shore immediately north of it to create the Mihama district; Chatan's own 2004 completion report for the project describes the two areas being planned as a single waterfront redevelopment from the start, with the coast formally zoned for recreation and tourism in 1987. The town settled on the concept that would define the site — an entertainment and shopping district styled after an American seaside town — in 1992, and construction began in earnest in 1997, with shops and attractions opening in stages from the following year until the complex now known as Mihama American Village was substantially complete by 2004.

The result sits deliberately close to what it replaced: a Ferris wheel, cinemas, restaurants and beachfront shops now occupy ground that was a US Marine Corps airfield within living memory, on a reclaimed shoreline immediately next to bases that, a few hundred metres inland, still occupy roughly half the town.

Little of pre-war Chatan is visible at street level, which makes Chatan Gusuku's limestone walls worth the climb: unlike the vanished paddies below it, the castle's terraces and one-metre-plus walls survive largely as archaeologists have mapped them, predating by three centuries the airfield that would later reshape everything around it. Fenced perimeters remain the town's most persistent visual fact — Kadena Air Base's boundary, Camp Zukeran's, Camp Kuwae's — and comparing them with the pre-war extent of the old "Chatan Tabukwa" paddies is one of the more direct ways to see how much of the historic farmland this dossier's aerial photographs sit on now lies behind a fence rather than under a plough.

Where the fence has moved, as at Hamby, the change is total: a wartime and Cold War runway is now a grid of shopping streets and a public marina, a transformation the town itself presents as proof that returned base land can be redeveloped successfully — while making plain, in the same official accounting, how much more of Chatan has not yet followed it.

timeline.what: Chatan Gusuku is built and used as a regional stronghold of the Chuzan kingdom on the coastal ridge above Chatan.
The earliest known written reference to the place-name Chatan, according to the town's own history.
Noguni Sokan, from the hamlet of Noguni in the Chatan magiri, brings the sweet potato from China; the kingdom formally commends his achievement in 1764.
A Satsuma-compiled map of the Ryukyu Kingdom labels the district "Kitatan magiri", the name that would evolve into "Chatan".
Nan'yo Shoko, a monk from Chatan's Tamayose hamlet remembered as "the Elder of Chatan", studies in mainland Japan.
Okinawa's magiri-to-village reform turns Chatan's twelve hamlets into aza of the new Chatan village.
US carrier aircraft raid Okinawa; 33 people are recorded killed in Chatan village.
US forces land on the coast around Chatan and Kadena; the village's farmland is soon cleared for a military airfield.
Kadena, its access across the expanding airfield now barred, separates from Chatan village as its own municipality (population about 3,800).
Okinawa reverts to Japan; about 65 percent of Chatan's area remains under US bases.
Hamby Airfield and the May-Moscarella firing range are returned to Chatan.
The town adopts the American Village concept (1992) and builds it out on the former Hamby and newly reclaimed Mihama land, substantially complete by 2004.
Town data put US base land at about 51.6 percent of Chatan's 13.91 square kilometres.
Chatan Gusuku is designated a national Historic Site.

walk.name: Chatan Gusuku
walk.what: Climb the coastal ridge to see the castle's five walled enclosures, cut and roughly coursed limestone masonry, and the view along the coast the fortress once guarded; a national Historic Site since 2021.

walk.name: Site of the Chatan Tabukwa paddies
walk.what: The low ground inland of the old village centre once carried paddies ranked among Okinawa's three finest rice tracts; compare the aerial photographs in this dossier to see how completely base construction and later urban development erased them.

walk.name: Kadena Air Base perimeter
walk.ja: 嘉手納飛行場フェンス
walk.what: The fence line marks ground taken from Chatan and Kadena village farmland from 1945; the base's scale is best appreciated from a public vantage point along its edge rather than from the base itself.

walk.name: Mihama American Village
walk.ja: 美浜アメリカンビレッジ
walk.what: Shops, cinemas and a Ferris wheel now stand on the returned Hamby Airfield and adjoining reclaimed land; look for the marina, built into the old airfield's redevelopment plan from the start.

walk.name: Sunabe seawall
walk.what: The coast road and seawall north of American Village front another of the old magiri's twelve hamlets, Sunabe, today better known for its dive sites and its view of Kadena Air Base's runway lights after dark.

caveats: Two official-adjacent sources give slightly different dimensions for Chatan Gusuku (about 165 m versus 30-100 m north-south); this dossier follows the Agency for Cultural Affairs' national designation record.
The claim that Chatan Gusuku ranks among Okinawa's largest gusuku comes from the town's own tourism/heritage page alone and was not cross-checked against an independent ranking.

Casualty figures here are limited to what an official Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications record states for the 10 October 1944 raid (33 dead in Chatan); no verified figure for deaths in the 1 April 1945 landing itself was found in a source read for this dossier.

Base land-share percentages are given exactly as reported for their own dates (65 percent in 1972, 68 percent for the mid-1970s planning era, about 51.6 percent as of town data current to 2018); a single fetch of a base-facilities page found in this session did not carry a more recent figure.
